| `obj2` | `cuboid` | `mass = 3`, `half_extents = [0.5, 1, 2]`, `position = [ 6, 0, 0]`, `angular_velocity = [0.01, 0.01, 3]` |
| `obj3` | `cuboid` | `mass = 3`, `half_extents = [0.5, 1, 2]`, `position = [-6, 0, 0]`, `angular_velocity = [3, 0.01, 0.01]` |
| `obj4` | `cuboid` | `mass = 3`, `half_extents = [0.5, 1, 2]`, `position = [ 0, 0, 0]`, `angular_velocity = [0.3, 3, 0.1]` |
| `obj5` | `cuboid` | `mass = 3`, `half_extents = [0.5, 1, 2]`, `position = [ 6, 0, 0]`, `angular_velocity = [0.01, 0.01, 3]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`cuboid`** — a uniform rectangular block. `I = (m/3) * diag(b^2+c^2, a^2+c^2, a^2+b^2)` for half-extents `(a, b, c)`. Three distinct moments in general, which is what makes a cuboid able to tumble. Half-extents are measured from the centre, so the full side lengths are twice these numbers.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`half_extents`** — half the side lengths, as `[a, b, c]`, measured from the centre. The full block is `2a` by `2b` by `2c`.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`angular_velocity`** — the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is OFF** (`g_constant = 0`). The simulator's default is 1, so this had to be said explicitly; without it, bodies that are supposed only to bounce or to be held by joints would also attract each other.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
eom:
There are 6 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = 0

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- nothing: every body coasts freely.
constraints:
**This model has no joints.** Nothing algebraic relates the coordinates, so the system is an ordinary differential equation rather than a differential-algebraic one, and it needs no Lagrange multipliers and no constraint Jacobian.

That does not mean nothing is conserved. Energy, linear momentum and angular momentum are still exact consequences of the equations of motion, and comparing them before and after a run is the honest way to judge the integration.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 6 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
6 bodies x 13 numbers = 78 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

There are no algebraic constraints, so the whole of the mechanics above is one first-order system

```
dy/dt = f(t, y),   y in R^78
```

handed to the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

The right-hand side `f` unpacks `y` into bodies, computes every force and torque, and packs the derivatives back in the same 13-per-body order.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.g_constant = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.rtol = 1e-12` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `rtol` is the integrator's relative error tolerance. Smaller is more accurate and slower. Joints that grip orientation impose a floor of `1e-6`, because the index-2 accuracy ceiling is real and asking for more produces convergence failures rather than better answers.

The value expected here is `1e-12`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.atol = 1e-14` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `atol` is the integrator's absolute error tolerance, which is what governs components passing near zero, where a relative tolerance means nothing. Orientation joints impose a floor of `1e-8`.

The value expected here is `1e-14`. A successful `set` prints nothing.
steps.code:
sim.do("set system.g_constant = 0")
sim.do("set system.rtol = 1e-12")
sim.do("set system.atol = 1e-14")

steps.title: Measure
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`get` evaluates an expression and prints it. The form is `GET <expression>`, where an expression may name a body's field (`obj0.position`, `bob.velocity.x`), index into it, or combine several with arithmetic and the built-in functions `norm`, `normalize`, `dot`, `cross`, `sqrt` and the rest.

Here it evaluates:

```
obj0.inertia_tensor
```

The corresponding Python call `sim.get(...)` returns the value as a Python object instead of printing it, which is what you want when the number is about to be used in a calculation.

---

`angmom` prints the total angular momentum about the origin, including both the spin of each body and the orbital contribution of its motion about the origin. With no external torque it is exactly conserved. It takes no arguments.

---

`energy` prints the total kinetic plus potential energy of the whole system. Take it before and after a run: for a closed system with no dissipation the two should agree to near machine precision, and how well they agree is the honest measure of the integration. It takes no arguments.

steps.explain:

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`run 2` advances the simulation by **2 seconds of duration** — not to absolute time 2. This trips people up: `run 1.7` followed by `run 2.89` leaves you at t = 4.59, not at 2.89. The form is `RUN <duration> [STEPS <n>]`.

`steps 1` asks for the result to be reported at 1 equally spaced points across that interval. It does not set the integrator's internal step size — SUNDIALS chooses that itself from the error tolerances, and takes as many internal steps between reports as accuracy demands.

This is the cell that actually integrates, so it is the slow one. It prints the time reached and how many internal solver steps were needed.

steps.title: The graphical scene window
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`scene create` opens the graphical scene window. It starts a small HTTP and WebSocket server — hand-rolled on `std::net`, with no web framework — and prints the address to open in a browser. The window shows the bodies as wireframes, with a readout of energy, momentum and angular momentum that updates live.

The window evolves its **own copy** of the system. Stepping in the notebook does not move the window, and playing the window does not move the notebook. That isolation is deliberate.

If the environment variable `POSIM_NO_BROWSER` is set, the address is printed but no browser is launched — which is what happens when this notebook is run non-interactively.

steps.title: The graphical scene window (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> 0.03 per tick at ~27 ticks/s -> a reversal cycle every ~10 wall-seconds.

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`scene set_time_step 0.03` controls the graphical scene window. The scene command family covers `CREATE`, `START`, `PAUSE`, `REVERSE`, `RESET`, `REFRESH`, and the camera controls.

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- `energy` was printed. Compare the value before the run with the value after it. For a closed system with no dissipation they should agree to near machine precision, and the size of the disagreement is the honest measure of the integration — not a number to be talked around.
- `angmom` was printed. With no external torque the total angular momentum about the origin is exactly conserved. Note that `L` is conserved, not `omega`: for a body whose three moments of inertia differ, the spin axis moves even though the angular momentum does not.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

Routh II.Art.155 — the three principal axes do NOT possess equal degrees of
stability — dynamic notebook

E. J. Routh, "The Advanced Part of a Treatise on the Dynamics of a System of
Rigid Bodies", Part II (Macmillan, 6th ed. 1905), Art. 155: "If a body be set
in rotation about any principal axis at a fixed point, it will continue to
rotate about that axis as a permanent axis. But the three principal axes at
the fixed point do not possess equal degrees of stability."

Art. 155a gives the geometry: about the greatest or least axis "the
neighbouring polhodes are ellipses" -- closed curves, so a disturbed axis
stays near. About the MEAN axis they are not, and the instantaneous axis
"will travel far".

THE LINEARISED PROOF. Order the principal moments A > B > C. Spin about the
mean axis B at rate n and let the other two components be small. Euler's
equations (Art. 137) give, to first order,

A*d(e_A)/dt = (B - C)*n*e_C          C*d(e_C)/dt = (A - B)*n*e_A

so   d^2(e_A)/dt^2 = [ (B - C)(A - B) / (A*C) ] * n^2 * e_A

With A > B > C both brackets are POSITIVE, so the coefficient is positive and
the solution is exponential: e^(kt). Repeat about the greatest axis and the
bracket becomes (B - A)(C - A)/(B*C) -- a product of two negatives over a
positive, hence negative -- and the solution is trigonometric. Same for the
least axis. Exponential growth versus bounded oscillation: that is the whole
difference, and it comes from one sign.

THIS BODY. A cuboid of mass 3 with half-extents (0.5, 1, 2) has

I = diag(5, 4.25, 1.25)      so   A = 5 (x),  B = 4.25 (y),  C = 1.25 (z)

Spun about y at n = 3, the growth rate is

k = n*sqrt((B-C)(A-B)/(A*C)) = 3*sqrt(3*0.75/6.25) = 3*0.6 = 1.8

an e-folding time of 0.56 -- so a disturbance of a few percent reaches order
unity within about three time units, and the body turns over.

READ THE AXIS IN THE BODY, NOT IN SPACE. This is the trap. The angular
momentum is fixed in space and the world-frame angular velocity stays close
to it, so watching world-frame omega_y shows NOTHING -- it sits near +3
forever. Routh's reversal is a statement about the body. The cells therefore
extract w_body = conj(q) * w_world * q with the quaternion product, and it is
the y-component of THAT which reverses.

MEASURED BEHAVIOUR (this notebook, gravity off, rtol 1e-12):

spun about y (MEAN):     body w_y = -1.15, -3.00, +1.43, +3.00, -1.67, ...
at t = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 -- a full reversal cycle
about every 8 units, forever
spun about x (GREATEST): |w - (3,0,0)| stays below 0.018 for 40 units
spun about z (LEAST):    |w - (0,0,3)| stays below 0.090 for 40 units

A NOTE ON THE PERTURBATION. The disturbance here is (0.3, 3, 0.1), chosen to
sit clearly OFF the separatrix G^2 = B*T of Art. 184. A symmetric disturbance
such as (d, n, d) is a trap with these particular moments: then
G^2 - B*T = A*d^2*(A-B) + C*d^2*(C-B) = d^2*(5*0.75 + 1.25*(-3)) = 0
identically, putting the motion exactly ON the separatrix, where the reversal
time is governed by rounding rather than by physics. Here G^2 - B*T = +0.3,
comfortably away from it.

SETUP NOTE. system.g_constant is set to 0. The three bodies must not attract
one another: pairwise gravity is on by default with G = 1, and although
gravity applies no torque, letting the bodies fall together drives the
separation towards the 1/r^2 singularity and wrecks the integration.

WHAT YOU WATCH: three identical boxes, spun at the same rate about their
three different principal axes. Two of them turn steadily and quietly. The
middle one tumbles end over end, again and again -- while its energy and
angular momentum never change by a part in 1e10.
